headline: Big night for US tech stocks as GOOG, MSFT and TTWO all surged last night — but the RBA rate hike to a 15-year high is the story every Aussie needs to read today.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO had a strong night last session, up 3.26%. The buzz around GTA 6 is building fast — Rockstar officially revealed three new gameplay details and even sent a care package to a major YouTuber, stoking hype. The game remains one of the most anticipated releases in history, and sentiment around Take-Two is riding that wave. Still down about 10% overall on your position, but the long-term GTA 6 thesis is very much alive.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google jumped 3% last night, pushing your position to a 13% overall gain. News that Anthropic's IPO filing revealed nearly 50% of its revenue flows through Amazon and Google highlights just how central Google's cloud infrastructure is to the AI boom. Strong session with no negative catalysts — the AI tailwind for Google remains intact.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft climbed nearly 2% last night, adding to solid overall gains of 17% on your position. No single headline drove it — the broader tech and AI rally lifted the whole sector. Microsoft continues to benefit from its deep OpenAI partnership and enterprise AI rollout. Steady as she goes.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS barely moved today, down just 0.26% at the ASX close. Analysts are still questioning whether the stock faces more share price pressure given lithium prices remain subdued. The long-term lithium outlook (a forecast 22.74% annual growth in the carbonate market through to 2031) is encouraging, but near-term pain continues. Your position is down about 43% overall — a tough hold, but the structural EV story hasn't gone away.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: No price data available for today's ASX session — VDHG didn't trade or data wasn't captured. As a broadly diversified fund, it would typically track the global market mood, which was positive last night in the US. Nothing to act on here.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: No price data for today's session. Emerging markets are worth watching given the ongoing Middle East tensions and their effect on oil prices and inflation globally, but no specific catalyst for VGE today.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: No ASX price data today for VTS. Given the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both rose solidly last night, VTS should see a positive flow-through when it next prices. The US market tail wind is blowing in the right direction.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: No price data today for GXAI. The AI sector was broadly strong last night — GOOG up 3%, MSFT up 2% — so the underlying holdings in this ETF likely had a good night. The AI safety pact signed by all the major players today (Google, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI) keeps the sector in focus.

watch_today.title: RBA hikes to 15-year high — mortgage pain incoming
watch_today.detail: The RBA lifted the cash rate to its highest level since 2011 and the major banks have already passed it on. This directly raises mortgage repayments for millions of Aussies and tightens consumer spending. For your portfolio, higher rates weigh on growth stocks and ETFs in the short term — but for a long-term holder, stay the course. The bigger risk is whether this tips the economy into a sharper slowdown.

watch_today.title: TTWO — GTA 6 hype building fast
watch_today.detail: Take-Two is still down about 10% on your total investment, but last night's 3.26% jump reflects growing GTA 6 momentum. Rockstar officially revealed three new gameplay details and is actively marketing the game. The release is the core thesis for holding TTWO — sit tight and let it play out.

watch_today.title: GOOG — strong session, Anthropic IPO reveals Google's cloud dominance
watch_today.detail: GOOG rose 3% last night and your position is up 13% overall. The Anthropic IPO filing showing nearly 50% of Anthropic's revenue flows through Google's cloud is a bullish signal — it shows Google is deeply embedded in the AI supply chain even when rivals benefit. Nothing to do here except enjoy the ride.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — still under pressure, but hold the line
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals slipped another 0.26% today and is down 43% on your investment. Analysts are questioning near-term price direction given soft lithium prices. But a new market report forecasts 22.74% annual growth in the lithium carbonate market through to 2031. The long-term EV story is intact — this is a painful hold, not a sell.

watch_today.title: Oil pushing toward $91 — watch inflation and the RBA
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) rose 1.79% last night to $90.98/barrel — the highest in a while. The Australian Treasurer is already pointing to Middle East conflict as a driver of local inflation. Dearer oil means higher petrol prices, more CPI pressure, and potentially more RBA rate hikes. Keep an eye on this — it matters for your cost of living and the broader market.

watch_today.title: MSFT — steady gains, AI story intact
watch_today.detail: Microsoft rose nearly 2% last night, now up 17% on your total position. No dramatic news — just steady AI-driven momentum from its OpenAI partnership and enterprise products. Classic long-term hold.

world.summary: A big day of global news — Middle East tensions remain elevated as Iran warns against Netanyahu's UAE visit, Trump launches a government AI chatbot that contradicts his own claims, oil hits multi-month highs, and JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon pitches a US-Europe free trade deal to counter China.

stories.title: Iran Warns of 'Dangerous Consequences' Over Netanyahu's UAE Trip
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has issued a stark warning that Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu's visit to the United Arab Emirates will have 'dangerous consequences.' This comes as tensions in the Middle East remain extremely elevated following the Iran-Israel conflict. The UAE and Israel normalised relations under the Abraham Accords, but Iran sees any deepening of those ties as a direct threat. This kind of diplomatic friction keeps the risk of further escalation alive — and with oil already above $90/barrel, any fresh flare-up could push energy prices even higher, hitting Aussie petrol prices and inflation.

stories.title: Tehran Still Waiting on US Response to Ceasefire Proposal Trump Already Rejected
stories.why_it_matters: Iran says it is still expecting a formal US response to a ceasefire proposal that the Trump administration has already publicly rejected. The diplomatic disconnect is significant — Tehran appears to believe talks are still possible, while Washington has moved on. Meanwhile, a separate report notes the US may permanently close some Middle East military bases damaged in the Iran conflict. That would represent a major shift in American military posture in the region after decades of heavy presence.

stories.title: Middle Eastern Oil Exports Hit Highest Level Since Iran War Began
stories.why_it_matters: Despite the ongoing conflict, Middle Eastern oil exports have risen to their highest level since the Iran war started — a somewhat counterintuitive development that suggests producers are pushing hard to capitalise on elevated prices. Oil (WTI) closed last night at $90.98/barrel, up nearly 2%. For Australians, this flows through directly to petrol prices and broader inflation, giving the RBA more reason to keep rates higher for longer. It's also a reminder that energy markets can surprise — more supply doesn't always mean cheaper oil when geopolitical risk is high.

stories.title: Trump Launches America.gov AI Chatbot — That Contradicts His Own Claims
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration launched a new government website called America.gov, featuring an AI chatbot powered by official government data. The awkward twist: the bot's answers — drawn from real government statistics — directly contradict several of Trump's public claims on topics like trade, jobs, and the economy. It's an unusual situation where the government's own AI tool is fact-checking the president. The chatbot is also funded by taxpayers, with critics pointing out it's being used for what looks like political advertising.

stories.title: Jamie Dimon Pitches US-Europe Free Trade Deal to Counter China
stories.why_it_matters: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon — one of the most powerful voices in global finance — publicly proposed a 'big, beautiful' free trade agreement between the US and Europe, calling it an 'economic NATO' to counter China's growing influence. It's not policy yet, but when Dimon speaks, markets and politicians listen. A US-Europe trade deal would be a massive shift in global commerce, potentially reshaping supply chains, currency flows, and investment patterns. For Australian investors, it's a signal that the world's biggest economies are thinking seriously about economic blocs — and where that leaves countries like Australia trading with both sides.

markets.summary: Last night was a solid night for US markets — tech led the charge with NASDAQ up 1% and the S&P 500 gaining 0.56%. Gold hit a new high above $4,210/oz. Oil is pushing toward $91. The Aussie dollar slipped against the USD, falling 0.85% to 69.57 US cents — partly on RBA rate hike uncertainty and broader USD strength. ASX 200 data wasn't available at time of publication.

politics.summary: The RBA lifted the cash rate to its highest level since 2011 — the dominant story in Australian politics and economics today. The major banks have already passed on the hike, and there's a fierce political blame game underway about who's responsible for Australia's inflation problem.

stories.title: RBA Raises Cash Rate to Highest Since 2011 — Banks Pass It On Immediately
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has lifted the official cash rate to its highest point since 2011 — a level not seen in 15 years. Australia's major banks wasted no time, passing the full hike on to mortgage holders. This means higher monthly repayments for anyone with a variable home loan, and increased financial pressure on households already stretched by the cost of living. The RBA has flagged the decision was driven by persistently high inflation, partly linked to rising oil prices from the Middle East conflict.

stories.title: Treasurer Points to Middle East Conflict as Inflation Driver
stories.why_it_matters: The Federal Treasurer has publicly attributed a significant portion of Australia's inflation problem to rising oil prices driven by the Iran conflict in the Middle East — pushing back on criticism that government spending is the primary cause. The political blame game is heating up, with the opposition arguing Labor's spending is fuelling inflation while Labor points offshore. Economists are divided, but the practical effect on households is the same: higher prices and now higher mortgage rates.

stories.title: Economists Warn RBA Hike Risks Sharper Economic Slowdown
stories.why_it_matters: Multiple economists are warning that the RBA's decision to push rates to 15-year highs risks tipping the Australian economy into a sharper-than-expected slowdown. The concern is that rate hikes work with a lag — the full impact of previous hikes may not have fully hit households yet, and adding another on top could cause a hard landing. For investors, a slowing Aussie economy is worth watching — it could affect corporate earnings, consumer spending, and the ASX's direction in coming months.

stories.title: Guardian: 'Stop the Inflation Blame Game and Let the RBA Do Its Job'
stories.why_it_matters: Economist Saul Eslake, writing in The Guardian, argues that the political point-scoring over inflation is counterproductive and that both sides of politics should step back and let the RBA operate independently. He contends that inflation has multiple causes — global energy prices, supply chain issues, and yes, some domestic spending — and that scapegoating either party misses the point. The key takeaway: don't expect a quick rate cut — the RBA is likely to stay hawkish (meaning rate-hike biased) for a while yet.

ai.summary: A massive day in AI news — the major tech companies signed a voluntary AI safety pact with the Trump administration, OpenAI scrapped a new model over safety concerns and instead launched new AI 'agents' called Dots, and Australia's banking regulator announced a review of AI use in financial services.

stories.title: Google, OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, Nvidia Sign Trump's Voluntary AI Safety Pact
stories.why_it_matters: Every major AI company — Google, OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, and Nvidia — has signed onto a voluntary AI safety agreement brokered by the Trump administration. But critics are calling it 'grading each other's homework': there are no binding legal requirements, no independent enforcement body, and the companies themselves decide what counts as safe. The accord notably leaves out mandatory disclosure of training data, safety testing results, or liability frameworks. Supporters say it's a start; sceptics say it's a PR exercise that lets the industry self-regulate on its own terms.

stories.title: OpenAI Scraps GPT-6.1 Astra Launch Over Safety Concerns, Releases 'Dots' Agents Instead
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI cancelled the planned launch of GPT-6.1 Astra — its next-generation AI model — because internal safety testing flagged concerns it wasn't ready. Instead, the company launched a new product called 'Dots': a set of small, capable AI agents designed to handle specific tasks autonomously (think: booking appointments, managing files, or running searches without you having to guide them step by step). Dots are being positioned as a rival to Meta's Muse agents. The scrapping of GPT-6.1 is actually a positive sign — it shows OpenAI is taking safety gates seriously rather than rushing to market.

stories.title: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic Subpoenaed to Testify at NYC Council Hearing on AI Risks
stories.why_it_matters: The New York City Council threatened to subpoena (legally compel) the CEOs of OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and Meta to appear at a hearing on AI risks — and all four agreed to attend after the threat was made. City lawmakers are concerned about AI's impact on jobs, housing discrimination, surveillance, and consumer privacy. It's a sign that even as the federal government goes soft on AI regulation, local governments are stepping in. For investors in GOOG and MSFT, regulatory scrutiny of AI is a slow-burning risk worth monitoring.

stories.title: Australia's Banking Regulator to Review AI Use by Banks
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's prudential regulator (APRA — the body that oversees banks and insurers) has announced a review into how Australian banks are using AI and the risks it poses to customers. The review will examine things like automated lending decisions, fraud detection, and customer service chatbots. It's an early-stage review rather than new rules, but it signals the regulator is paying close attention. For everyday Aussies, it's worth knowing that the AI your bank might be using to approve or deny your loan is now under the microscope.

sport.summary: NRL Grand Final week is here — Roosters vs Knights on Sunday at Accor Stadium. Meanwhile, there's Judiciary drama with a key ban confirmed, Dally M Awards hype is building, and the AFL world is buzzing with Lachie Neale trade news.

stories.title: Roosters vs Knights Grand Final Set for Sunday 6:30pm at Accor Stadium
stories.why_it_matters: It's Grand Final week! The Sydney Roosters take on the Newcastle Knights at Accor Stadium this Sunday, October 4, with kick-off at 6:30pm. Silverchair — the iconic Newcastle band — has reportedly responded to the Knights' pleas to perform at Grand Final festivities, adding some rock-and-roll flavour to what would be a historic Knights victory if they pull it off. This is the biggest game of the NRL season.

stories.title: Crossland Cops Four-Game Judiciary Ban, Apologises to Cleary
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL Judiciary handed down a four-game ban to Crossland following a foul play charge — a significant suspension that will sideline him into the early part of next season. Crossland issued a public apology to Nathan Cleary (presumably the victim of the incident), calling himself 'remorseful.' The ban is done and dusted heading into the Grand Final, so it won't affect Sunday's game, but it's a notable disciplinary outcome for the season's final week.

stories.title: Dally M Awards: When They Are, How Voting Works, and Who's Favourite
stories.why_it_matters: The Dally M Medal — the NRL's best player award — will be announced this week as part of Grand Final festivities. Fox Sports has released its ultimate guide to the night, covering who the contenders are, how the voting system works (points are awarded by match officials after each game throughout the season), and who's considered the frontrunner. No specific winner named yet, but it's one of the highlights of Grand Final week for NRL fans.

stories.title: Rabbitohs Re-Sign Young Gun Before November 1 Free Agency Window
stories.why_it_matters: South Sydney Rabbitohs have locked in a young gun to a contract extension ahead of the November 1 free agency window, when players off contract can speak to rival clubs. Retaining developing talent before that window opens is a smart move by the Bunnies. No specific player name available from the headlines, but it signals the Rabbitohs are already planning aggressively for 2027.

stories.title: Lachie Neale '48 Hours' From Major Life Change — Brisbane Lions AFL Star in Trade Limbo
stories.why_it_matters: Brisbane Lions captain and two-time Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale is reportedly just 48 hours away from making a major life decision — widely reported to be a trade request or a surprise contract renewal. Multiple outlets have described it as an 'extraordinary revelation,' with Neale apparently close to a deal that mirrors his current contract ('same deal'). He is one of the AFL's biggest names, and his decision will be one of the most talked-about stories of the trade period.
